title: Islamic Civil Calendar
intro: This is a calculated, or tabular, Islamic lunar calendar. Its dates are worked out using a repeating arithmetic rule, so no observation of the crescent Moon is needed to determine a month.
summary: Twelve lunar months, usually alternating 30 and 29 days. A calendar year contains 354 or 355 days.
origin: The arithmetic civil convention is one way to calculate Hijri dates. The model here uses the project's documented Friday-epoch rule and is distinct from local crescent-based religious calendars.
structure: Each lunar month is shorter than a typical solar month. The civil calculation usually alternates between 30 and 29 days; some years add a day to the final month.
pattern_note: A regular mathematical leap pattern determines when the final month has 30 rather than 29 days. This keeps civil calculations reproducible without Moon sighting reports.
history: Muslim societies have used more than one method of determining Hijri dates. Computed tables are useful for records and planning, but actual religious observance can follow local crescent reports or a particular authority.
example: Ramadan is the ninth month. Its date in a civil table may differ from a community's Ramadan start announced after observing or accepting a crescent sighting.
limits: This tabular civil calendar is not a prediction of the actual crescent's visibility, not a universal religious ruling, and not a substitute for local historical evidence.
